concepts.description: A collection of autonomous computers interconnected to exchange information.
A software system that makes independent networked computers appear as one coherent system.
A communication model in which clients send requests and servers return replies.
A communication model without fixed clients and servers, where peers exchange data directly.
A set of rules governing the format and meaning of messages exchanged by peer entities.
A set of operations that a layer provides to the layer above it.
The boundary that defines how one layer accesses services of another layer.
The organization of network functions into layers, each using services below and serving layers above.
A set of protocols used by a system, one protocol per layer.
A specification of layers and protocols sufficient to implement network communication.
The process of wrapping data with protocol headers and trailers as it moves down the stack.
Control information added to data by a protocol layer.
Control information appended to the end of a frame or packet.
A formatted unit of data carried by a packet-switched network.
A data unit transmitted by the data link layer.
A transport-layer data unit, especially in TCP.
A self-contained packet delivered independently in a connectionless service.
A service that establishes a connection before data transfer and releases it afterward.
A service in which each message is sent independently without establishing a connection.
A service that uses acknowledgements or recovery mechanisms to avoid data loss.
A seven-layer reference model for open systems interconnection.
A layered model based on the Internet protocol suite.
A practical model with physical, link, network, transport, and application layers.
The layer responsible for transmitting raw bits over a physical medium.
The layer that sends frames across a directly connected link with error and flow control mechanisms.
A data link sublayer that controls access to a shared transmission medium.
The layer responsible for routing packets across networks and internetworks.
The end-to-end layer that provides transport services such as reliable byte streams or datagrams.
The layer containing protocols used directly by networked applications.
An OSI layer for establishing, managing, and synchronizing sessions.
An OSI layer concerned with syntax, semantics, and encoding of transmitted information.
A short-range network for devices around one person.
A privately owned network within a limited area such as a building or campus.
A network that covers a city-scale area.
A network spanning a large geographical area such as a country or continent.
A network that uses radio or other wireless media for communication.
A wireless network designed to support mobile users.
The global internetwork that uses TCP/IP protocols to connect many networks.
A collection of interconnected networks, often using routers or gateways.
A network portion or addressing subdivision, depending on context.
A computer attached to a network that runs applications and exchanges data.
A network-layer device that forwards packets between networks.
A link-layer device that forwards frames between ports.
A device that connects networks and may translate between different protocols or layers.
A link-layer device that connects LAN segments and forwards frames.
A physical-layer device that regenerates and forwards signals.
A simple device that broadcasts incoming link-layer signals to all ports.
A device that connects wireless clients to a wired or wireless network.
An organization that provides Internet connectivity to customers.
A location where customer traffic enters an ISP network.
A facility where ISPs connect and exchange traffic.
A high-capacity core network that interconnects routers and networks.
A facility containing many networked servers and supporting infrastructure.
The frequency range or data capacity available for communication.
The number of bits transmitted per unit time.
The time taken for data to travel or be delivered across a network.
The effective rate at which data is successfully delivered.
Variation in packet delay over time.
A measure comparing signal power with noise power.
A theoretical limit on data rate for a noiseless bandwidth-limited channel.
The maximum reliable data rate of a noisy channel.
The process of encoding digital data onto signals for transmission.
Transmission using signals directly over a medium without carrier modulation.
Transmission by modulating data onto a carrier frequency.
The sharing of a communication medium by combining multiple signals or flows.
Multiplexing that divides a channel into frequency bands.
Multiplexing that divides a channel into time slots.
Multiplexing in which users share spectrum using different codes.
A multicarrier modulation technique widely used in wireless and broadband systems.
Physical or wireless media used to carry signals.
A guided transmission medium made of pairs of twisted copper wires.
A guided transmission medium with a central conductor and shielding.
A transmission medium that carries signals as light through glass or plastic fiber.
Wireless transmission using radio-frequency electromagnetic waves.
A network that uses satellites to relay communication signals.
The process of dividing a bit stream into frames.
Mechanisms that detect or recover from errors in transmitted data.
Techniques for detecting corrupted data.
Techniques for recovering correct data from corrupted transmissions.
A compact value used to detect transmission or storage errors.
An error-detecting code based on polynomial division.
An error-correcting code that uses parity bits to detect and correct bit errors.
Mechanisms that prevent a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver.
A control message indicating successful receipt of data.
An event used to trigger retransmission when an expected response is not received in time.
Sending data again after loss, corruption, or timeout.
A reliability method that retransmits data when errors or losses are detected.
A protocol that sends one frame and waits for its acknowledgement before sending the next.
A protocol family that allows multiple outstanding frames within a moving window.
A sliding window protocol that retransmits a lost frame and all subsequent frames.
A sliding window protocol that retransmits only missing or corrupted frames.
The problem of deciding which sender may use a shared communication channel.
A random access protocol family for shared channels.
A multiple access method in which stations sense the carrier before transmitting.

concepts.description: A wireless MAC method that attempts to avoid collisions.
An event where simultaneous transmissions interfere on a shared medium.
A dominant family of wired LAN technologies and link-layer protocols.
Ethernet using switches and point-to-point links rather than a shared bus.
A link-layer hardware address used to identify interfaces on a LAN.
A bridge or switch that learns which addresses are reachable through which ports.
A protocol that prevents loops in bridged Ethernet networks.
A logical LAN that partitions a physical LAN into separate broadcast domains.
A family of wireless LAN technologies based on IEEE 802.11.
A frame format used in IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs.
A short-range wireless technology often used for personal area networks.
A technology for identifying objects using radio-frequency tags and readers.
A switching method that forwards data in packets over shared networks.
A switching method that reserves a dedicated circuit for communication.
A switching method in which a node receives a complete packet before forwarding it.
A switching method that begins forwarding before a full packet has been received.
A connection-oriented network-layer abstraction with a path set up before data transfer.
A network in which each packet is routed independently.
The process of determining paths for packets through a network.
The local action of sending a packet from an incoming interface to an outgoing interface.
A table used by routers to decide where to forward packets.
Routing based on paths with minimum cost according to a metric.
A routing method that sends packets on many or all outgoing links.
A distributed routing algorithm in which routers exchange distance vectors with neighbors.
A routing algorithm in which routers flood link-state information and compute paths locally.
Routing that scales by organizing routers or networks into hierarchy.
Routing that delivers packets to all destinations in a network.
Routing that delivers packets to a selected group of receivers.
Routing that delivers packets to one of several equivalent destinations.
Mechanisms to prevent or respond to overload in a network.
Mechanisms that provide service guarantees or differentiation for network traffic.
Techniques for regulating traffic patterns to meet network constraints.
A mechanism that decides whether new flows may enter the network.
Encapsulating packets of one protocol inside another to traverse a network.
Splitting packets into smaller fragments and reassembling them later.
The largest packet or frame size that can be transmitted over a link or path.
Version 4 of the Internet Protocol, widely used for packet addressing and forwarding.
Version 6 of the Internet Protocol, with a larger address space and extension headers.
A network-layer address used to identify interfaces or hosts in IP networks.
Dividing an IP address space into smaller subnetworks.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing, an IP address allocation and routing method using prefixes.
A mechanism that maps private addresses to public addresses, often at a gateway.
A protocol that maps IP addresses to link-layer addresses on a local network.
A companion protocol to IP used for control and error messages.
A protocol that automatically assigns IP configuration to hosts.
A packet forwarding technique that uses labels instead of long network-layer lookups.
A link-state interior gateway routing protocol.
The interdomain routing protocol used to exchange reachability between autonomous systems.
A collection of IP networks under common administrative control for routing.
A protocol for supporting host mobility while preserving IP communication.
The service provided by the transport layer to applications or upper layers.
An API abstraction used by applications to communicate over the network.
A transport-layer identifier used to distinguish application endpoints.
Using port numbers to combine and separate traffic for multiple applications.
The process of creating a transport connection before data transfer.
The process of closing or releasing a transport connection.
The TCP procedure for establishing a connection using SYN and ACK messages.
A reliable, connection-oriented transport protocol that provides a byte stream.
A connectionless transport protocol that provides lightweight datagram delivery.
The control fields attached to TCP segments.
TCP's window mechanism for flow control and reliable delivery.
TCP mechanisms for adapting sending rate to network congestion.
A TCP state variable limiting how much data may be in flight due to congestion control.
A TCP congestion-control phase that increases the congestion window rapidly from a small value.
The time for a packet to travel to a destination and for a response to return.
TCP mechanisms for estimating timeouts and managing retransmissions.
A protocol for carrying real-time audio and video streams.
A communication abstraction that lets programs invoke procedures on remote machines.
A distributed naming system that maps domain names to network information such as IP addresses.
A human-readable name used to identify hosts or services.
A DNS database entry containing name mapping or related information.
A server that answers DNS queries.
The application protocol used to request and transfer Web resources.
HTTP protected using TLS or SSL for confidentiality and authentication.
A string that identifies the location of a resource on the Web.
A distributed hypertext system using HTTP and related technologies.
A client application that retrieves and displays Web resources.
A server that responds to HTTP requests.
An intermediary server that forwards requests or caches content.
A small piece of state stored by a browser for Web applications.
An application for exchanging messages between users over networks.
A protocol for sending and relaying email messages.
An email retrieval protocol for downloading messages from a mail server.
An email access protocol that manages messages on a server.
A format extension for carrying non-ASCII and multimedia content in email and HTTP.
An application protocol for transferring files between hosts.
An early remote terminal protocol.
A distributed infrastructure that delivers content from servers close to users.
Audio or video delivered continuously over the network for playback.
Voice communication carried over IP networks.
A signaling protocol often used to set up voice and video sessions.
A peer-to-peer protocol for distributed file sharing.
Techniques and protocols for protecting network communication.
The study and use of techniques for secure communication.
Cryptography in which sender and receiver share the same secret key.
Cryptography using mathematically related public and private keys.
A public-key cryptosystem based on the difficulty of factoring large integers.
A widely used symmetric block cipher standard.
An older symmetric block cipher standard.
A function that maps data to a fixed-size digest, often for integrity checks.
A cryptographic mechanism for authenticity and integrity.
A signed statement binding a public key to an identity.
The infrastructure for issuing, managing, and validating public-key certificates.
The process of verifying an entity's identity.
The security property that prevents unauthorized disclosure of information.
The security property that prevents undetected modification of data.
A suite of protocols for securing IP packets.
Protocols for securing transport connections, especially HTTPS.
A security system that filters or controls network traffic.
A private network abstraction built over a shared network, often using tunneling and encryption.
An authentication system based on a trusted key distribution center.
A protocol for establishing a shared secret over an insecure channel.
A modern version of HTTP with multiplexed streams over a single connection.
A modern version of HTTP that runs over QUIC.
A UDP-based transport protocol used by HTTP/3.
A networking architecture that separates the control plane from the data plane.
